transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-27
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 52m
Recording: yes
Attendees: Samira Ortiz (Redwood, AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood, SE), Priya Shah (Nimbus, ML Platform Lead), Marcus Lee (Nimbus, SRE), Daniela Ruiz (Nimbus, CTO)

Summary (auto):
Redwood and Nimbus ran through a technical deep dive focused on quantization compatibility and stability across INT8, FP8, GPTQ and AWQ codepaths. Discussion included observed accuracy regressions, KV cache interactions, batching and warmup effects, and options for canary/fallback strategies in a VPC/on-prem deployment. Next steps agreed to run targeted benchmarks on customer data and deliver a canary plan plus security docs.

Topics:
- Regression surface: which prompt types and layers are most sensitive
- Runtime codepaths differences (AWQ vs GPTQ vs INT8 mixed)
- KV cache staleness / warmup and batching interaction
- Canary/fallback design: per-layer fallback, precision cascade, sticky KV coalescing
- VPC/on-prem constraints and profiling hooks

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samira Ortiz: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro — i'm Samira, the AE, and Ethan is our infra SE. today we want to walk through what we saw in your packet with the INT8 snapshot and the regression notes.
[00:12] Priya Shah: thanks, Samira. we saw a consistent drop on summarization outputs when moving to awq int8, about 3–6% on rouge-l nails. curious what the first pass hypothesis should be.
[00:27] Ethan Cole: yeah, thanks Priya. quick caveat — our transcription of your logs had a couple mis-ids but the numbers are clear. first thing we look at is layer sensitivity; often top transformer layers and feedforward weights trigger semantic drift. for AWQ specifically the rounding strategy can bias certain tokens.
[00:44] Marcus Lee: can you explain the difference in runtime between awq and gptq on our onprem stack? we've got A100s and some T4s in a different cluster.
[00:56] Ethan Cole: sure. gptq tends to produce less per-layer noise because the calibrations are per-tensor-block; AWQ uses a different kernel with stochastic-ish rounding heuristics which can reduce model-size but introduces edge-case token shifts. Runtime: AWQ kernel in our runtime uses fused GEMM paths that are faster on Ampere but the fp8 path — when mixed — can have different memory access patterns that increase latency variance if KV cache isn't warm.
[01:18] Daniela Ruiz: latency variance is the big one for us, SLOs are 150ms p95 for short-chat flows. does Redwood recommend dedicated or hosted for best SLO?
[01:30] Samira Ortiz: for strict p95 sub-150 you typically want dedicated capacity with pinned GPUs and our lowest-latency model variants. on-prem is possible but you need careful kernel tuning and we usually do a small canary to validate. this call is exactly that — figure out which fallback to use if int8 causes drift but reduces cost.
[01:48] Priya Shah: we also saw kv-cache staleness causing hallucinations for follow-ups, especially under batching. manifest looked like responses that referenced old context. any ideas?
[02:00] Ethan Cole: KV cache staleness often happens if the sticky-kv policy isn't aligned with batch coalescing. if you're doing aggressive batching and reordering, the KV indices can map to stale keys. we recommend enabling per-request KV tagging in the runtime and a short kv-warmup window for the first 2–4 tokens when using mixed precision. also some quant paths zero-out small residuals differently which exacerbates token drift.
[02:26] Marcus Lee: is that a config toggle or code change? we prefer config where possible.
[02:30] Ethan Cole: mostly config: batching window, per-route kv tagging, and a precision-fallback table. two code changes we've pushed in the past are a kv-coalescer that preserves ordering and a precision-gating layer that will auto-fallback to a higher precision for problematic layers. we can provide both as options in the canary.
[02:48] Priya Shah: can you walk us through a concrete canary plan? we want to minimize customer impact while validating accuracy and latency.
[02:55] Samira Ortiz: sure — high level: 1) baseline runs (FP16) with your prompt set to capture metrics; 2) run INT8/AWQ/GPTQ variants on a 1% traffic shadow and run diffs on token and embedding level; 3) enable per-layer fallback for top 6 layers and measure regression delta; 4) roll to 10% with KV warmup policy and measure p50/p95; 5) if regressions over threshold, auto-fallback to fp16 for affected model-version. we'll instrument trace headers so you can map tokens to layers.
[03:35] Daniela Ruiz: what's the practical cost delta between int8-awq and a fp16 fallback? our finance team wants ballpark numbers.
[03:42] Samira Ortiz: depends on throughput. ballpark: INT8/AWQ quantized paths can reduce GPU memory and token cost by ~2.2–2.8x versus fp16. fallback to fp16 for small percent of requests increases cost maybe 10–30% relative to fully quantized, depending on percent of fallbacks. we can run a cost sim with your traffic profile.
[04:02] Priya Shah: on accuracy metrics — we saw particular failures in code-generation-like prompts and multi-sentence summarization. is that typical?
[04:10] Ethan Cole: yes, code and structured outputs are high sensitivity because they rely on exact token sequence likelihoods. quantization can slightly change logits that break deterministic sequences. GPTQ tends to be more stable for code gen but larger on-disk. AWQ/INT8 can be tuned layerwise to retain higher precision in residuals for the first and last few layers which helps.
[04:34] Marcus Lee: you mentioned layerwise gating — how coarse is it? per-layer only or per-weight-block?
[04:40] Ethan Cole: our runtime supports per-layer gating and in dynamic mode per-attention-head gating is experimental. practically we do per-layer gating with a threshold on KL divergence for a small eval set. The gating table can say: layer 1–3 use INT8-AWQ, layers 4–24 use GPTQ-fine, last 2 layers FP16. That combination kept throughput high while stabilizing outputs in previous pilots.
[05:05] Priya Shah: what about evaluation — you referenced token-level diffs, embedding divergence, and human evals. what's the minimum suite you'd recommend?
[05:12] Ethan Cole: min suite: 1) token-level diff and edit-distance across prompt types, 2) embedding cosine similarity on representative queries, 3) focused human eval set for post-edit correctness for code and summarization. we also add a latency-lift test to check p95 regressions under peaky traffic.
[05:30] Daniela Ruiz: are regression alerts possible in the Redwood console? we want automated detection.
[05:34] Samira Ortiz: yes — Redwood Optimize can flag quality regressions against a golden prompt set and trigger alerts. you can tie alerts to rollout policies that automatically revert or trigger per-layer fallbacks. we'll demo that in the next session.
[05:48] Priya Shah: the logs we shared had weird tokenizer mismatches — sometimes tokenization differences made diffs noisy. any advice?
[05:55] Ethan Cole: make sure the tokenizer and bpe merges are identical; even small differences in unicode normalization cause diffs. we recommend shipping a tokenizer snapshot and running byte-level checksums at canary start.
[06:08] Marcus Lee: we run in a VPC with strict egress. how heavy are the profiling hooks you suggested? do they need extra ports?
[06:16] Ethan Cole: profiling hooks are lightweight. we can stream traces to your internal ingest via an HTTPS endpoint or S3, AES encrypted. If egress is blocked, we can provide an on-prem agent that writes to an internal store. hooks typically add ~1–3% CPU and negligible latency when sampling at 1%.
[06:36] Priya Shah: in earlier pilots we saw cold-start latency due to kv-warmup when scaling from zero — any mitigation suggestions?
[06:42] Ethan Cole: pre-warming KV caches at the node level and using sticky sessions helps. also incremental warmup: respond to the first few tokens synchronously and then allow batching after the warm window. another mitigation is hybrid caching where hot prefixes are kept in a small LRU on faster memory.
[07:02] Daniela Ruiz: let's talk about the most surprising regression cause in your experience — anything non-obvious?
[07:08] Ethan Cole: one non-obvious is scheduler jitter in multi-tenant nodes: when mixed precision code paths change memory footprints, CUDA scheduler can re-prioritize kernels and you get micro-tail spikes. We instrumented and observed p95 jumps that only appeared with certain quant combos and particular batch sizes. Fix was to isolate quantized workloads or pin cgroup CPU for the inference threads.
[07:32] Priya Shah: hmm that maps to what we saw. we also had a case where token alignment change triggered a downstream reranking model to misfire. it's messy.
[07:39] Samira Ortiz: yeah those secondary model interactions are why we recommend end-to-end chain testing for multi-model stacks.
[07:46] Marcus Lee: about the codepaths — are your AWQ/GPTQ implementations deterministic across runs? our strict reproducibility requirement is a blocker.
[07:54] Ethan Cole: GPTQ deterministic if quant seeds and calibration are fixed; AWQ historically had non-deterministic rounding unless you force deterministic kernels. we have toggle to force deterministic math but it can cost 5–8% throughput. we can help you evaluate tradeoffs.
[08:12] Priya Shah: ok, can you show an example of the token-diff output we should expect?
[08:18] Ethan Cole: sure — we'll generate a sample diff in the results spreadsheet. typical diff artefacts: small insert/delete near punctuation, token swaps in low-prob alternatives, and occasionally truncated completions if kv-warmup misses.
[08:32] Samira Ortiz: pointer — we uploaded a proposed canary checklist and a benchmarking sheet, link is here: https://redwood-internal.shared/canary-checklist (note: placeholder link). also the security pack will include KMS integration notes, egress requirements, and audit log retention.
[08:52] Priya Shah: great. can you talk about fallback thresholds — what would you recommend for our SLO and regen tolerances?
[08:58] Ethan Cole: for Nimb's 150ms p95 and critical correctness on summarization, recommend conservative thresholds: token-level edit distance > 0.06 or embedding cosine < 0.985 triggers per-layer fallback. for human-facing classification maybe tighter. we can tune after the first run.
[09:20] Marcus Lee: will the fallback cause spikes in latency when it happens?
[09:24] Ethan Cole: yes potentially — a fallback to FP16 is slower per request. to mitigate we use progressive fallbacks: first try per-layer precision bump (only a few layers), if still bad then full FP16. also queue shaping to keep p95 bounded.
[09:40] Priya Shah: any known incompatibilities with off-the-shelf tokenizer libs for onprem windows? we use a mix of linux and windows containers.
[09:49] Ethan Cole: windows containers can have path and unicode normalization gotchas; ensure your tokenizer library uses utf-8 normalization and consistent BPE merges. we can provide an init container that verifies tokenizer checksums.
[10:02] Priya Shah: ok, what's the expected deliverable from the next run?
[10:06] Samira Ortiz: we'll deliver a shared spreadsheet with token-diffs, embedding stats, latency distributions, and a recommended fallback mapping (table). also a canary run playbook describing traffic split, KV warmup, metrics to watch, and rollback criteria.
[10:20] Daniela Ruiz: timeline acceptable. do you need infra access to run the benchmarks or will you run on our artifacts?
[10:26] Ethan Cole: prefer artifact-driven to avoid egress — if you can provide the 10k token sample and prompt sets we'll run locally in our staging that matches your hw profile. if you prefer on-prem runs we can provide the canary package for you to run with a simple script.
[10:44] Priya Shah: we'll try artifact-driven first. sending prompts and sample by Monday.
[10:48] Samira Ortiz: great. quick question — any legal or procurement blockers we should be aware of?
[10:53] Daniela Ruiz: procurement wants SOC2 and KMS details before any pilot that touches PII. also, we need to know if we can enable HSM-backed keys.
[11:01] Samira Ortiz: understood — i'll include SOC2 report, KMS/HSM integration notes and a minimal dataflow diagram in the security pack.
[11:08] Marcus Lee: one last technical: under what circumstances would you recommend FP8 over INT8 or vice versa?
[11:15] Ethan Cole: FP8 is attractive for models that already have attention numeric sensitivity and where you want to preserve dynamic range; it's faster for certain hw that has native fp8 kernels. INT8 (with awq/gptq variants) is denser and often cheaper but more brittle on certain token distributions. we often pick FP8 for large seq gen and INT8/AWQ for high-throughput chat where cost matters.
[11:36] Priya Shah: ok that helps.
[11:38] Samira Ortiz: wrapping up — agreed next steps and action items captured. we'll follow up with results and the canary plan. any final questions?
[11:46] Daniela Ruiz: no, thanks everyone. looking forward to the results.
[11:49] Marcus Lee: thanks.
[11:50] Ethan Cole: thanks all.
[11:52] Samira Ortiz: bye.
